title: The Trap Closes: Moab, Judah, and Israel
summary: Amos finishes the circle of neighbors with Moab, then turns to Judah for rejecting the LORD's law, and finally to Israel. Israel sells the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, tramples the poor, abuses a young woman, and lounges at its altars on garments taken from debtors. God recalls all he did for Israel, from the exodus to the prophets and Nazirites, and announces a judgment from which not even the strongest and swiftest will escape.
story: Chapter 1 condemned Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon, and Amos's northern hearers would have agreed with every word. Chapter 2 adds Moab and then Judah, Israel's southern rival, which would still have pleased them. Then the prophet names Israel, and the longest and most detailed indictment of all falls on his audience. The chapter is the hinge of the book's opening: it shows that God's people are held to the same justice as the nations, and to a higher standard because of all they have received. What follows in chapters 3 to 6 unfolds these charges.
historical:
The Moabite crime of burning the bones of Edom's king is not recorded elsewhere in the Bible. Some connect it with the wars between Moab and its neighbors in the ninth century BC (2 Kings 3 describes a campaign in which Israel, Judah, and Edom fought Moab together), but the specific event is unknown. Kerioth was an important Moabite town, mentioned also in the Mesha Stele, a ninth-century inscription in which Mesha king of Moab describes his wars with Israel.

The charges against Israel describe the social world of Jeroboam II's prosperous kingdom around 760 BC. Wealth was concentrating in the hands of officials and landowners in and around Samaria, while small farmers were vulnerable to debt after a bad harvest. A family could lose its land and then its members could be sold into servitude to pay creditors. The law allowed debt service but limited it and protected the debtor (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12-15; Leviticus 25:39-43). Some scholars regard the oracle against Judah (verses 4 and 5) as a later addition, since its charges are more general than the others; others see it as integral, since leaving out Judah would weaken the point that no one escapes.
cultural:
Several of Israel's crimes refer to laws its hearers knew. The law required that a garment taken as a pledge for a loan be returned to a poor man by sunset, because it was his only covering at night (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-13). Amos pictures creditors keeping those cloaks and stretching out on them beside the altar at religious feasts, and drinking wine bought with fines exacted from the poor, in the very "house of their God". To "sell the righteous for silver" probably means selling into slavery people who were in the right, whether through corrupt courts or merciless debt collection. Selling the needy "for a pair of sandals" may mean for a trivial debt; some interpreters connect sandals with transfers of land (Ruth 4:7) and read it as a picture of seizing a poor family's property.

Verse 7 accuses a man and his father of having relations with the same girl. The Hebrew word means a young woman, and many interpreters think she was a servant in the household, exploited by both men; others think Amos refers to ritual sex at a shrine. On either reading the act was forbidden (Leviticus 18:8, 15) and exploited someone who could not refuse. Nazirites (verses 11 and 12) were Israelites who took a vow of special dedication to God that included abstaining from wine (Numbers 6); to make them drink was to mock their consecration.
literary: Verses 1 to 5 continue the formula of chapter 1 exactly: the numerical saying, the charge, the fire. Verse 6 begins the same way with Israel, but then the pattern breaks. Instead of a single charge there is a list (verses 6 to 8); instead of an immediate threat of fire comes a recital of God's past kindness (verses 9 to 11), introduced by an emphatic "Yet it was I". The contrast between what God did and what Israel did is the heart of the indictment. The closing threat (verses 13 to 16) is built from a string of seven warriors who will fail: the swift, the strong, the mighty, the archer, the fleet of foot, the horseman, and the bravest, who will flee naked.

outline.t: Moab: burning the bones of Edom's king
Judah: rejecting the law of the LORD
Israel: selling the needy and abusing the weak
What God did, and how Israel answered
No escape, even for the strongest

doctrines.note: Judah is condemned for rejecting "the Law of the LORD", and Israel's crimes break specific commands about pledges, debt, and sexual conduct. The law was not an abstract code but a protection for the vulnerable, and to ignore it was to abandon them.

Sin in this chapter is concrete and social: selling people, trampling the poor, exploiting a young woman, and doing it while worshiping. Amos also shows sin's deeper root in ingratitude, as Israel forgets everything God has done.
Israel is judged by the same God who judges the nations, and its privileges do not exempt it. The judgment described is total: strength, speed, and skill all fail.

words.note: Evyon, needy. It describes someone in want, dependent on others, often in debt. The law repeatedly commands open-handed care for the evyon (Deuteronomy 15:7-11), and Amos uses the word four times in his book for those the powerful are crushing.

Dal, poor, weak, or low. The word can describe physical weakness, but in Amos it names people with little land or power who are easily pushed aside. Their heads are trampled into the dust, a picture of contempt as well as oppression.

Chaval, to take something in pledge as security for a loan. The law regulated this practice carefully, forbidding creditors to take a millstone or to keep a poor man's cloak overnight. Amos's hearers would have recognized the reference instantly.

Nazir, a Nazirite, one consecrated or set apart. The Nazirite vow (Numbers 6) was voluntary and could be lifelong, as with Samson and Samuel. God names Nazirites alongside prophets as gifts he gave Israel, living signs of devotion that Israel corrupted.

christ: Amos's charges against Israel find echoes in Jesus's own warnings. Jesus condemned religious leaders who "defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers" (Mark 12:40), the same combination of piety and exploitation that Amos saw at Israel's altars. The chapter's recital of God's grace (the exodus, the land, the prophets) followed by his people's ingratitude anticipates Jesus's parable of the tenants, who beat the servants sent to them and finally killed the owner's son (Mark 12:1-12). Amos also shows why the gospel is good news for the poor. The God who takes the side of the needy against those who trample them is the God who, in Christ, came to proclaim good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). These are thematic connections; Amos is not predicting Christ here, but he describes the God Jesus revealed.

hard.q: Is Amos condemning wealth itself or the way it was gained?
hard.a: Readers have taken Amos in different directions, so it helps to look at exactly what the text says. The charges in this chapter name specific acts: selling people into slavery for money or small debts, trampling the poor, sexual exploitation, keeping pledged cloaks the law said must be returned, and drinking wine paid for by fines. Elsewhere Amos condemns bribery, rigged scales, and luxury enjoyed without grief for the nation's ruin. He does not condemn owning flocks (he may have owned them) or prosperity as such. His target is gain made by injustice and indifference to the vulnerable, especially by those with power over courts and markets. Some interpreters emphasize the systemic side, the way a whole society's arrangements allowed the strong to devour the weak; others emphasize personal responsibility for individual acts of cruelty and fraud. Amos holds both: the people he names made choices, and those choices together made a society God judged. He measures it all against Israel's covenant law, not against any modern economic or political program.

questions: God reminds Israel of everything he has done for them before naming their sins. How does remembering what God has done for you change the way you see your own failures?
The creditors in this chapter kept the letter of worship while breaking the law's protections for the poor. Where can religious practice become a cover for ignoring others' needs?
Israel silenced its prophets and corrupted its Nazirites. What voices of conscience or examples of devotion are easy to silence in your community?
